Triggers.value: Water, flooding, or large bodies of water

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

vignette: Kofi had always been a calm and collected individual, but that all changed on the fateful day his younger brother, Kwame, drowned while swimming in the lake near their family's village. It was a sunny afternoon, and Kofi had been walking along the shore when he saw Kwame struggling to stay afloat. He rushed into the water, but it was too late; by the time he reached him, Kwame had slipped beneath the surface. The memory of that moment was forever etched in Kofi's mind - the feeling of helplessness as he watched his brother disappear into the depths of the lake. In the months following the tragedy, Kofi began to notice changes within himself. He found himself becoming increasingly anxious whenever he encountered large bodies of water or even just heard the sound of running water. The smell of damp earth and algae, reminiscent of the lake's shore, would transport him back to that terrible day. Stress, too, seemed to trigger a cascade of physical reactions - his heart racing, muscles tensing, before he could even process what was happening. His body had become like a sentry on high alert, always ready to react to danger, but unable to distinguish between real and perceived threats. As the days turned into weeks, Kofi found it increasingly difficult to shake off the negative emotions that lingered long after the initial shock of his brother's death had worn off. Fear, horror, anger - they all swirled together in a toxic brew that left him feeling drained and exhausted. He tried to fill his days with work, throwing himself into his teaching duties as a professor, but even the familiar rhythms of academia couldn't calm his racing mind. Kofi's inability to relax had become particularly debilitating. Even when he was alone in his office or at home, surrounded by the comforting trappings of his daily routine, he felt on edge. He would try to focus on his lectures or grading papers, but his body seemed to be perpetually coiled, ready to spring into action at a moment's notice. Sleep became fitful and elusive, as if his mind was constantly scanning for potential threats. As the months dragged on, Kofi began to withdraw from social interactions, avoiding gatherings with colleagues or friends where he might encounter triggers - a pool party, a trip to the beach, even just a walk near the lake. His relationships began to fray, and his students started to notice a change in their normally affable professor. He felt like he was losing himself, becoming trapped in this prison of anxiety and hypervigilance. One day, while preparing for class, Kofi's eyes wandered out the window, where he spotted a group of students playing by the campus pond. The sight of the water sent his mind reeling back to that awful moment on the lake shore. Suddenly, it hit him - he couldn't keep living like this. He needed help to reclaim his life from the grip of PTSD. With a sense of trepidation and hope, Kofi made an appointment with a therapist, unsure what lay ahead but certain that he couldn't face another day trapped in this cycle of fear and anxiety.
